LESSON 31 OF 106·Cryptography Essentials

TLS: How a Secure Connection Is Negotiated

Follow a TLS 1.3 handshake message by message: where the session keys come from, how the server proves its identity, and which checks a client must never skip.

Foundation15 min
Why this matters

TLS is what makes HTTPS work. The handshake agrees on a protocol version, authenticates the server, negotiates keys, and only then does application data flow. Almost every step is a decision about what you refuse to accept.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • The client offers a list of protocol versions and cipher suites, and the server chooses one from that list.
  • Server certificates are presented and validated, which is how the client learns it is talking to the right host.
  • A key exchange derives fresh session secrets, so each connection has keys that are never transmitted.
  • With modern versions the key exchange can itself be authenticated, so no separate certificate round trip is needed.
  • Finished messages verify that both sides derived the same keys and detected tampering, before any application data is sent.

The background

  • SSL was designed for the web in the 1990s and had a long list of design and implementation problems.
  • TLS 1.2 improved on it but still allowed negotiation to fall back to weaker options, which is what downgrade attacks exploited.
  • TLS 1.3 removed the problematic negotiation, shortened the handshake, and removed algorithms that were long known to be weak.
  • Encrypted client hello, now being adopted, hides the last plaintext detail, which was the server name in the initial request.

Real-world examples

  • A server that still supports an old protocol version remains downgradeable even if modern clients prefer a new one.
  • A captive portal that intercepts traffic typically presents a certificate the client is asked to accept, which is the moment trust is given away.
  • Certificate pinning left in place after a key rotation causes an outage that is often mistaken for an attack.

What to look for

  • Check that only current protocol versions are enabled and that weak cipher suites are removed.
  • Confirm the server presents a certificate for the exact name being visited.
  • Check that forward secrecy is in use and that legacy renegotiation is disabled.
  • Check the certificate chain is complete, because an incomplete chain fails for some clients and not others.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

OWASP Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet

Auditing a TLS configuration against current guidance on protocol versions, cipher suites, certificate lifecycle and validation requirements

Open OWASP resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Enable only current protocol versions and a short list of strong cipher suites.
  • Serve HSTS so browsers refuse to fall back to an unencrypted connection.
  • Automate certificate issuance and renewal, including the intermediate certificates.
  • Monitor for protocol downgrade attempts and for clients reporting certificate errors.
  • Remove obsolete options such as legacy renegotiation, which exist for compatibility nobody should still need.
